content: The Open Source Center (OSC) is a United States government agency that specializes in analyzing open-source materials, including gray literature, through its domestic and international bureaus. It was officially established on November 1, 2005, under the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI). The primary mission of the OSC is to enhance the accessibility and utility of open-source information for intelligence officers and other government officials. The OSC also provides materials to the National Technical Information Service (NTIS) and other government entities via its online news service, World News Connection. In 1992, Senator David Boren, who was then the Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, introduced the National Security Act of 1992 in an effort to implement moderate reforms within the U.S. Intelligence Community. Congressman Dave McCurdy, his counterpart on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, supported the legislation. The House version of the bill included a proposal for a separate Open Source Office, an idea suggested by Larry Prior, a Marine Reservist with experience in the Marine Corps Intelligence Center (MCIC) and a staff member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. In 1996, the Aspin-Brown Commission reported that U.S. access to open-source information was severely deficient and emphasized that addressing this issue should be a top priority for funding and the attention of the Director of Central Intelligence (DCI). Later, in July 2004, the 9/11 Commission recommended the establishment of an open-source intelligence agency, though it did not provide specific details or guidance on its structure. Subsequently, in March 2005, the WMD Commission (also known as the Robb-Silberman Commission) recommended the creation of an Open Source Directorate within the CIA. Following these recommendations, the Director of National Intelligence announced the establishment of the DNI Open Source Center in November 2005. The OSC was tasked with collecting information from a wide range of openly available sources, including the Internet, databases, press, radio, television, video, geospatial data, photographs, and commercial imagery. Beyond information collection, the OSC was also responsible for training analysts to effectively utilize open-source information in their work. The OSC incorporated the CIA's pre-existing Foreign Broadcast Information Service (FBIS), which had been operational since 1941. Douglas Naquin, who had been the head of FBIS, was appointed as the director of the newly formed Open Source Center.
